newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's de Klerk attacks ANC over violence.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's de Klerk attacks ANC over violence.

text.p: South Africa's former white president F.W. de Klerk, buoyed by the acquittal of his defence minister in a landmark murder trial, accused the ruling African National Congress on Friday of hiding the skeletons in its own closet.

"If you watch television, listen to the radio or read newspapers sympathetic to the ANC, then it seems like the ANC were angels," de Klerk said in remarks prepared for delivery to a congress of his National Party in Free State province.
"The overwhelming majority of deaths as a result of political violence resulted from black on black violence," he said.
"Unfortunately we have seen little effort to get to the bottom of the ANC's involvement in the conflict -- the massive intimidation, violence and necklace murders of black opponents."
Earlier on Friday, a judge acquitted former defence minister Magnus Malan of 13 murder charges arising from a 1987 massacre in KwaZulu-Natal province.

The judge found the killing was almost certainly carried out by members of the Inkatha Freedom Party, which had received support from the then white-led government, but said no direct link to Malan had been proved.
An estimated 15,000 blacks have been killed in political violence in the province which broke out between Inkatha and the ANC in the mid-1980s.
ANC leaders have accused a "third force" comprising members of the white security establishment of orchestrating the violence and condemn use of the term "black-on-black violence".
De Klerk told members of his party, the largest opposition group in parliament, that files containing serious allegations against ANC leaders had not been investigated by Mandela's government.
"Tonight I ask President Nelson Mandela, Deputy President Thabo Mbeki and Justice Minister Dullah Omar to tell the nation what they are going to do about this," he said.
If the files were to remain closed, then "the ANC is misusing its power within the government to carry out a witch hunt among its opponents".
De Klerk said he particularly wanted to know who in the ANC had given the orders for two guerrilla bomb attacks in Durban and Pretoria in which white civilians were killed or maimed.
"We demand action against the prominent ANC figures who are implicated in serious violations of human rights and who, on the face of it, are being protected by the ANC government," de Klerk said.
Earlier he welcomed Malan's acquittal and said he should never have been brought to trial in the first place.
